name: Fraxel (Fraxel Restore / Dual)
lead: Fraxel is a trademarked line of fractional laser systems for skin resurfacing, built on the principle of fractional photothermolysis: laser energy is delivered as an array of microscopic columns, leaving the skin between them untreated so that healing is faster than with full-surface lasers [1]. Fraxel Restore and Fraxel Dual are non-ablative models using a 1550 nm erbium fiber laser, with the Dual adding a 1927 nm thulium wavelength for more superficial pigment targets [1].

Fractional laser resurfacing is used in aesthetic medicine for photodamage, wrinkles, acne and surgical scars, and pigmentation such as melasma [2][4][5][6]. Published studies, mostly small clinical series, report improvement in these indications; a large series also catalogued side effects including acne flares and herpes outbreaks [3][9]. Within looksmaxxing discussion it is categorised as a professional "hardmaxx" skin-quality procedure.

paras: Fractional photothermolysis was described in 2004 by Dieter Manstein and Rox Anderson at the Wellman Center for Photomedicine, as a way to produce microscopic thermal injury zones with less downtime than ablative lasers [1]. Reliant Technologies licensed the concept and launched the first Fraxel system in 2004; Reliant was later acquired in a deal that created Solta Medical, which introduced the Fraxel re:store Dual in 2009 and was itself acquired by Bausch Health in 2014, according to Grokipedia [1]. That account is AI-generated and has not been independently checked here.

A 2007 study reported use of fractional photothermolysis for atrophic scars [2], and a 2006 Japanese trial examined it for acne scars [6]. A 1,550 nm fractional erbium fiber laser was studied for facial and non-facial photodamage [5], and a 2005 pilot study examined melasma [4]. A comparison in Asian patients tested different fluences and densities for skin rejuvenation [7]. These studies are small and short-term, and results for melasma in particular have been described as variable.

A study of 961 fractional treatments documented complications including acne eruptions and herpes simplex outbreaks, and noted that anecdotal reports describe scarring and pigment change [3][9]. Grokipedia describes redness and swelling for one to three days followed by peeling [1].

Human studies include case series on atrophic scars [2], acne scars [6], photodamage [5] and melasma [4], a split-parameter comparison in Asian skin [7], and a safety review of 961 treatments [3]. Registered trials include a 100-person comparison of lasers for scars [8] (outcomes not summarised here) and withdrawn trials for hair loss. Most published work consists of small, often industry-linked series without long-term controls.

timeline.event: Fractional photothermolysis described at the Wellman Center; first Fraxel launched and cleared by FDA [1].
Fraxel re:store Dual (1550/1927 nm) introduced by Solta Medical [1].
Solta Medical acquired by Bausch Health [1].

card.summary: The original branded fractional laser for scars, photodamage and melasma, with decent small-study support and a multi-session, several-day recovery.
card.aka: Fraxel re:store, Fraxel Dual, Fraxel FTX
card.note: Side effects documented include acne flares, herpes outbreaks and pigment change.

quick.overview:
Fraxel is a brand of fractional lasers that treat microscopic columns of skin, aiming to stimulate collagen and refresh texture, scars and pigmentation. It is performed in clinics in a series of sessions.

Published research consists mostly of small studies on scars, photodamage and melasma reporting improvement.
quick.mechanism: Laser energy absorbed by water in tissue creates microscopic thermal zones; surrounding intact skin speeds healing and the body remodels the injured zones with new collagen [1].
quick.risks: Reported effects include redness, swelling, peeling, acne flares, herpes outbreaks and, more rarely, scarring or pigment changes [3][9]. It is a medical-device procedure performed by clinicians.
